extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of moral philosophy and history of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A historical-philosophical analysis and critique of utilitarian/inductive moral theories (especially Hartley, Bentham, Hutcheson, and their successors), focusing on the sources of moral motive, the role of conscience, association of ideas, and the adequacy of the 'greatest happiness' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is supported by different sanctions — religious, legal, social, physical/political/moral — that motivate conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky cites Paley, Locke, Bentham and others: e.g., Locke divides sanctions into 'Divine rewards and punishments, legal penalties and social penalties'; Bentham into 'physical, political, moral or popular, and religious.' These differing sanctions are portrayed as varying in kind and degree and are the motives by which 'ought' acquires meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of an unselfish element / sympathetic feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: A plausible moral theory must account for an unselfish or sympathetic element in human nature — the pleasure we take in others' joy and the reality of benevolent affections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter contrasts Hobbesian selfishness with Shaftesbury/Hutcheson and notes that later utilitarians recognized sympathetic pleasures; the presence, origin (innate vs associated), and motivational role of benevolence are central to evaluating theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of association of ideas (Hartley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral sentiments can be explained by association of ideas: things first valued as means become valued as ends by repeated association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hartley (and predecessors like Gay, Hutcheson anticipations) explain love of money, praise, virtue, etc., as arising when means to pleasure become associated with pleasure and thus loved for themselves; this doctrine is evaluated for its explanatory power and limits, and its heavy reliance on education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure derived from benevolence and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure obtained from acts of benevolence and sympathy is a key motive to virtue and must be recognized by any adequate account of morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilitarians admit pleasures of sympathy but differ on source (derived via association or original). The text stresses that cultivation of sympathetic feelings and 'the pleasure derived from their exercise' is a leading motive to virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as a real and ruling principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An acceptable moral theory should recognize conscience as a genuine motivating force that can be 'the ruling principle of our lives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hartley's school uniquely recognizes conscience as important and explains it as generated by association (love of virtue for itself). The formation, authority, and motivational primacy of conscience are treated as crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and power of education in moral formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, by shaping associations, has immense practical importance in forming dispositions and moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because association of ideas can make certain pleasures and praises be felt as ends, early education that links praise/pleasure with virtue will predispose one toward virtue; thus the theory emphasizes artificial formation of disposition via upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selfishness as the underlying motive (critique of reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory reduces all moral action to self-regarding pleasure/avoidance of pain, it is accused of rendering the notion of 'unselfish' conduct meaningless and at odds with common moral language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky argues it's reasonable to call actions selfish if motivated by avoiding suffering or seeking enjoyment, but he notes the moral repugnance and common-sense distinction between virtue and mere prudence that any such reduction must overcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with common moral language and sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral theory should not render common ethical vocabulary and intuitions (honour, justice, virtue vs prudence, interest) unintelligible or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky contends utilitarianism conflicts with universal everyday distinctions and popular judgments about self-sacrifice, so a successful theory must account for why ordinary moral vocabulary treats virtue as distinct from mere interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive matters versus consequences-only account
rubrics_metrics.description: A defensible moral theory must address whether the agent's motive is morally relevant — the utilitarian denial that motives influence moral value is critiqued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bentham's view that 'there is but one motive possible, the pursuit of our own enjoyment' and that motives should be excluded from moral judgment is examined and found to clash with moral intuitions that regard motive as diminishing or enhancing merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure of virtue must not be the object sought
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic satisfaction of virtue is argued to be obtainable only when not consciously sought as the motive; if the glow of satisfaction is the deliberate aim, it undermines the moral worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prayer and benevolence. If the worshipper or giver consciously seeks the inward benefit, the reflex moral benefit fails; conscience 'refuses to ratify the bargain' if duty done solely for anticipated pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional clarity of 'happiness' and the greatest-happiness principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral standard that rests on 'happiness' or 'greatest possible happiness' must offer a determinate, definable account; otherwise the standard is too indeterminate to serve as a precise moral test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky points out diversity of what nations or individuals consider happiness and the resulting impossibility of precisely defining the 'greatest possible happiness' as a consistent measuring rod.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of moral value to utility (and its paradoxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If utility alone measures virtue and vice, degrees of moral quality must strictly track degrees of utility, producing counterintuitive moral rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky argues this leads to odd conclusions: monstrous sensualities might produce less unhappiness than certain temperamental defects; gratitude vs revenge; and public leaders whose unscrupulous means yield benefits would be morally elevated if utility alone were the measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote consequences and the problem of secrecy/exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory that relies on consequences must reliably account for remote consequences, example effects, and whether secrecy can render a clearly harmful act morally permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky notes utilitarians reply that secret acts might be justified if no bad example ensues, but he questions whether a single secret act could be permitted if it yields immediate utility but undermines social bulwarks (sanctity of life/property), and examines the claim that habit/disposition formation counters this objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological plausibility: distinction between imagination and action
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate moral theory must distinguish between pleasures of imagination and the moral significance of action; mere imagined vice producing pleasure should not be equated with virtuous conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky warns that utilitarianism may license indulgence in vicious imagination since pleasure without action increases net utility; critics argue such phenomena show a theory needs to connect moral worth with action and conscience, not just hedonic calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of moral duties (including duty to animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral theory should coherently account for duties toward different classes of beings (e.g., animals) and explain their moral basis in a manner consistent with broader moral sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky treats the duty of humanity to animals as a topic utilitarianism can handle but which intuitive moralists explain via affections produced by circumstances; the theory is judged by how naturally it explains expansion of moral concern.
